question: Why is ILS classed as a precision approach aid?

options.text: It is accurate to within ±1° in azimuth at all ranges
It gives guidance in both the horizontal and vertical planes
It can be used down to touchdown in every category
It is the only approach aid monitored on the ground

explanation: A precision approach provides both lateral (localizer) and vertical (glide path) guidance. A VOR or NDB approach gives lateral guidance only and is non-precision.

question: What does the pilot decide at decision height (DH) on an ILS approach?

options.text: Land with the required visual references, or go around
To switch from the glide path to the PAPIs
To disconnect the autopilot and fly manually
To change from the localizer to the back beam

explanation: At DH the pilot continues to land only with the required visual references and room for a safe touchdown; otherwise the published missed approach is flown.

question: What are the three main ground components of an ILS?

options.text: Localizer, VOR and DME
Localizer, glide path and approach radar
Glide path, NDB and approach lights
Localizer, glide path and marker beacons

explanation: The localizer gives azimuth guidance, the glide path vertical guidance and the markers range checks. A locator NDB, a paired DME or a back course may be added.

question: Where is the localizer aerial normally sited?

options.text: At the outer marker, 4 NM from the threshold
About 300 m before the threshold on the centre line
About 300 m beyond the upwind end of the runway
Beside the runway, abeam the touchdown point

explanation: The localizer array is on the extended centre line at the far (upwind) end of the runway, about 300 m beyond it.

question: Where is the glide path aerial normally sited?

options.text: On the extended centre line before the threshold
About 300 m beyond the upwind end of the runway
About 300 m in from the threshold, 200 m to the side
At the middle marker, about 1 km from the threshold

explanation: The glide path transmitter is to one side of the runway, about 120–200 m from its edge, abeam the touchdown point roughly 300 m in from the threshold.

question: What is a locator in an ILS installation?

options.text: A DME giving range to the threshold
A UHF transmitter paired with the localizer
A VHF marker placed beyond the upwind end
A low-powered NDB co-located with the outer marker

explanation: A locator (L) is a low-power NDB, usually at the outer marker site, used to fly the approach pattern and check position.

question: What has increasingly replaced marker beacons for range information on ILS approaches?

options.text: A DME frequency-paired with the ILS
A back course on the reciprocal runway
A VOR on the localizer frequency
A second glide path on a different angle

explanation: A paired DME gives continuous range to the threshold, supplementing or replacing the markers' single-point checks.

question: In what band and frequency range does the localizer operate?

options.text: UHF, 329.15 to 335 MHz
VHF, 108 to 111.975 MHz
VHF, 108 to 117.975 MHz
VHF, 75 MHz only

explanation: Localizers use 40 channels between 108 and 111.975 MHz, shared with VORs. Glide paths are UHF (329.15–335 MHz) and markers are 75 MHz.

question: Which frequencies in the 108–112 MHz band are allocated to ILS localizers?

options.text: Even first decimals, and even decimals plus 0.05
Every 0.05 MHz between 108 and 112 MHz
Odd first decimals, and odd decimals plus 0.05
Only frequencies ending in 0.05

explanation: Localizers use odd decimals (108.1, 108.15, 108.3, 108.35…); VORs in the same band use even ones.

question: In what band does the ILS glide path operate?

options.text: SHF, about 5 GHz
VHF, 75 MHz
VHF, about 108 to 112 MHz
UHF, about 329 to 335 MHz

explanation: The glide path uses 40 UHF channels from 329.15 to 335 MHz, each paired with a localizer frequency.

question: On what frequency do all ILS marker beacons transmit?

options.text: 75 MHz
400 kHz

explanation: All markers use 75 MHz. Their narrow fan-shaped vertical beams stop them interfering with one another.

question: How does the pilot select the glide path frequency?

options.text: By selecting the DME channel first
Automatically, by tuning the paired localizer
Separately, on a dedicated UHF control box on the pedestal
By selecting the marker beacon receiver

explanation: Each glide path frequency is paired with a localizer frequency (e.g. 108.1 MHz with 334.7 MHz), so tuning the localizer also tunes the glide path.

question: Which is an advantage of pairing localizer and glide path frequencies?

options.text: One selection tunes both, with less chance of error
It doubles the number of ILS channels available
The two signals can be identified separately
The glide path can then be used without the localizer

explanation: Pairing means one switch for both receivers, quicker and simpler selection, fewer wrong selections and a single identifier.

question: How is an ILS identified?

options.text: Separate idents on the localizer and the glide path
A continuous tone on the localizer
2–3 Morse letters, usually starting with I, on the localizer
3 letters in Morse on the glide path only

explanation: Only the localizer carries an ident, 2 or 3 letters at about 7 groups a minute, usually beginning with "I". Pairing makes a separate glide path ident unnecessary.

question: What does a continuous tone, or no ident at all, on an ILS mean?

options.text: It is serviceable for Category III operations
Only the glide path is serviceable; fly the localizer by DME
The localizer is in back-course mode
It is under maintenance or test: do not use

explanation: When an ILS is withdrawn, under maintenance or radiating only for test, the ident is removed or replaced by a continuous tone. Its indications may be completely wrong.

question: The glide path is unserviceable but the localizer is radiating normally with its ident. What happens?

options.text: The ident is replaced by a continuous tone
ATC warns that it is localizer only
The ident changes to TST until the glide path is repaired
The localizer is switched off as well

explanation: The ILS may continue for localizer-only approaches with its normal ident; ATC warns users and the glide path must not be used.

question: Up to what height is a DME paired with an ILS protected?

options.text: 2 500 ft, on the final approach only
10 000 ft, within 10 NM of the threshold
50 000 ft, at any range
25 000 ft, within the localizer service area

explanation: The paired DME is protected within the localizer service area up to 25 000 ft (extended when notified for SIDs and STARs). Use outside these limits may be in error.

question: To what point are the ranges of an ILS-paired DME referenced?

options.text: The runway threshold
The glide path aerial
The localizer aerial
The outer marker

explanation: ILS DME ranges are zero-referenced to the threshold, so the DME reading is distance to the threshold rather than to the aerial.

question: What shape are ILS marker beacon radiation patterns?

options.text: Pencil beams aimed along the glide path
Narrow vertical fans, lens-shaped in plan
Omnidirectional at all heights
Cones with a cone of silence overhead

explanation: Markers radiate narrow fan-shaped beams straight up, appearing lens or bone shaped in plan. They are received only when flying through the fan and give no direction.

question: How is the outer marker indicated in the cockpit?

options.text: Blue light, 6 dots a second, 3 000 Hz
White light, 6 dots a second, 3 000 Hz
Blue light, 2 dashes a second, 400 Hz tone
Amber light, alternate dots and dashes, 1 300 Hz

explanation: OM: blue, two dashes per second, low-pitched 400 Hz. MM: amber, alternate dots and dashes, 1 300 Hz. IM: white, six dots per second, 3 000 Hz.

question: How is the middle marker indicated in the cockpit?

options.text: White light, 6 dots a second, 3 000 Hz
Amber light, continuous dashes, 400 Hz
Blue light, 2 dashes a second, 400 Hz
Amber light, alternate dots and dashes, 1 300 Hz

explanation: The middle marker shows an amber light with alternating dots and dashes at a medium pitch of 1 300 Hz.

question: How is the inner marker indicated in the cockpit?

options.text: Blue light, alternate dots and dashes, 400 Hz
Amber light, 6 dots a second, 1 300 Hz
White light, 6 dots a second, 3 000 Hz
White light, 2 dashes a second, 3 000 Hz

explanation: The inner marker has a white light and a high-pitched 3 000 Hz tone of six dots per second.

question: How far from touchdown is the outer marker typically sited?

options.text: 3.5 to 6 NM
1 to 2 NM
0.5 to 1 NM
8 to 10 NM

explanation: The outer marker is 6.5–11.1 km (3.5–6 NM) from touchdown, typically where the aircraft intercepts the glide path.

question: How far from the threshold is the middle marker typically sited?

options.text: About 300 m (1 000 ft)
About 1 050 m (3 500 ft)
About 4 NM
About 75 m (250 ft)

explanation: The middle marker is about 1 050 m ± 150 m from the threshold, roughly where a Category I aircraft would be at its DH.

question: How many marker beacons must each ILS installation have?

options.text: None, if a locator is fitted
Two, with a third if needed
Three, always
One, at the outer marker

explanation: Two markers (outer and middle) are required; an inner marker may be added at a particular site.

question: What is a Z marker?

options.text: A marker at the upwind end of the runway
The inner marker of a Category III ILS, closest to the runway
A cylindrical marker over a reporting point or NDB
A marker on the back course of a localizer

explanation: Z markers have cylindrical vertical patterns and mark airway reporting points or sit with an NDB, showing when the aircraft is overhead the beacon's cone of silence.

question: How must a marker used with a localizer back course be identified?

options.text: With an ident clearly different from the front-course markers
With a voice message giving the range
With a continuous tone and no light
With exactly the same ident as the outer marker

explanation: A back-course marker must be clearly distinguishable from the front-course markers so a pilot cannot confuse the two approaches.

question: For a Category I ILS, how far may the localizer shift at the reference datum before the monitor acts?

options.text: 20 ft
25 ft
50 ft
35 ft

explanation: The monitor acts if the localizer shifts from the centre line by more than 35 ft (Cat I), 25 ft (Cat II) or 20 ft (Cat III).

question: What change in glide path angle triggers the ILS monitor?

options.text: More than 0.75° from the published angle
More than 0.15° from the published angle
More than 0.45 × the glide path angle
More than 0.075 × the glide path angle

explanation: A change of more than 0.075 θ (about 0.23° on a 3° glide path) triggers the monitor.

question: What power reduction from an ILS transmitter triggers the monitor?

options.text: More than 15%
More than 50%
More than 25%
More than 75%

explanation: Any transmitter losing more than half its output power causes the monitor to act.

question: What can the ILS monitor do when a fault is detected?

options.text: Stop radiating, remove the ident, or downgrade
Increase transmitter power to compensate for the fault detected
Switch the ILS to a different frequency
Change the ILS to a back-course approach

explanation: The monitor warns the control point and may cease all radiation, remove the ident and navigation components, or allow a Cat II/III ILS to be used only to a lower category, before the standby takes over.

question: To what range must localizer coverage extend within ±10° of the centre line?

options.text: 10 NM
17 NM
25 NM
35 NM

explanation: Localizer coverage: 25 NM within ±10°, 17 NM between 10° and 35°, and 10 NM outside ±35° if coverage is provided.

question: To what range must localizer coverage extend between 10° and 35° from the centre line?

options.text: 25 NM
18 NM
10 NM
17 NM

explanation: Between 10° and 35° either side, coverage must reach 17 NM (31.5 km).

question: What is the minimum azimuth coverage of the glide path?

options.text: 10° each side of the centre line, to 25 NM
8° each side of the centre line, to 10 NM
35° each side of the centre line, to 17 NM
8° each side of the centre line, to 25 NM

explanation: The glide path must provide correct indications to at least 10 NM within 8° either side of the centre line.

question: Between what angles is the glide path's vertical coverage provided (θ = glide path angle)?

options.text: 0.45θ to 2θ

explanation: Coverage runs from 0.45θ up to 1.75θ above the horizontal. The lower limit may be reduced to 0.3θ to protect the glide path intercept procedure.

question: For a 3° glide path, between what angles must the glide path signal be usable?
explanation: 0.45 × 3° = 1.35° and 1.75 × 3° = 5.25°. The 0.9° figure would apply only if the lower limit were reduced to 0.3θ.

question: To what may the localizer coverage be reduced where other aids cover the intermediate approach?

options.text: 25 NM within ±35° only
10 NM within ±10°, and 5 NM elsewhere
18 NM within ±10°, and 10 NM elsewhere
17 NM within ±10°, and 25 NM elsewhere

explanation: When alternative navigation facilities give satisfactory coverage, the limits may be reduced to 18 NM within the ±10° sector and 10 NM in the rest of the coverage.

question: Is ILS energy radiated outside the published coverage sectors?

options.text: Yes, but correct indications are not guaranteed there
No, nothing is radiated outside them
Only at night, because of sky waves
Yes, and the indications are always correct

explanation: The coverage sectors are where correct indications must be provided. Energy exists outside them, but its indications may be misleading.

question: How are the two localizer lobes distinguished by the receiver?

options.text: The two lobes are transmitted alternately
The right lobe carries 90 Hz, the left lobe 150 Hz
The two lobes are on different VHF frequencies
The right lobe carries 150 Hz, the left lobe 90 Hz

explanation: Seen from the approach (inbound), the right-hand lobe is modulated at 150 Hz and the left-hand lobe at 90 Hz, on the same carrier.

question: What defines the localizer centre line?

options.text: Maximum depth of the 90 Hz modulation
Zero difference in depth of modulation (DDM)
Equal phase of the 90 Hz and 150 Hz signals
Maximum signal strength of the carrier

explanation: Depth of modulation increases away from the centre line. Where the 90 Hz and 150 Hz modulations are equal, the DDM is zero and the needle is centred.

question: An aircraft approaching the localizer from the right receives more 150 Hz than 90 Hz. What does the needle show?

options.text: Fly left
Centred
OFF flag
Fly right

explanation: Excess 150 Hz means the aircraft is right of the centre line (in the blue sector), so the needle shows fly left. Excess 90 Hz gives fly right.

question: Why is the back course of an ILS not used in the UK?

options.text: It is too narrow to fly accurately
It has no identification
It is on a different frequency from the front course
Reversed CDI sense, wrong glide path, no markers

explanation: A mirror-image localizer beam exists behind the aerial, but on a CDI its sense is reversed, the glide path would lead to the wrong end of the runway and there are no range-check markers. Ignore it in the UK.

question: How can an HSI give correct sensing on a back-course approach?

options.text: If the back course QDM is set on the course selector
If the front course QDM is set on the course selector
An HSI always gives reversed sensing on a back course
If the glide path receiver is switched off

explanation: The HSI corrects the sense when the front course inbound QDM is set; a basic CDI cannot and reads reversed.

question: When may back-course localizer guidance be used in the correct sense on a CDI?

options.text: For glide path guidance to the reciprocal runway
For a back-course approach to the reciprocal runway
For azimuth guidance on the missed approach
Never; it is always reversed on a CDI

explanation: Continuing straight ahead after a go-around, the aircraft is heading away from the localizer in the same direction as the approach, so the needle can be obeyed.

question: How are the two glide path lobes modulated?

options.text: Both lobes 90 Hz on different frequencies
Upper lobe 1 300 Hz, lower lobe 400 Hz
Upper lobe 90 Hz, lower lobe 150 Hz
Upper lobe 150 Hz, lower lobe 90 Hz

explanation: The glide path uses the same principle as the localizer in the vertical plane. Above the path 90 Hz dominates (fly down); below it 150 Hz dominates (fly up).

question: What range of glide path angles is permitted for ILS, and what is usual?

options.text: 2° to 4°, usually 3°
3° to 5°, usually 3.5°
2.5° to 3.5°, usually 3°
1° to 3°, usually 2.5°

explanation: The international standard requires the glide path angle to be between 2° and 4°. 3° is standard.

question: What is a false glide slope?

options.text: The back beam of the glide path behind the aerial
Another path of zero DDM, caused by repeated lobes
A glide path bent by heavy rain near the threshold
The path flown by an aircraft without a glide path receiver

explanation: Repeated lobes from reflections, metal structures and aerial characteristics create other paths where the DDM is zero.

question: At about what angle does the first false glide slope occur on a 3° ILS?
explanation: The first false glide slope is at about twice the glide path angle — around 6° for a 3° path. False glide slopes are always above the true one.

question: How is the danger of a false glide slope normally avoided?

options.text: Ignore the DME and follow the glide path needle
Intercept from below; cross-check height against range
Fly the approach with the glide path receiver off
Intercept the glide path from above at high speed

explanation: The usual practice is to establish on the localizer and intercept the glide path from below. Where it is captured from above, height must be confirmed against distance using DME, markers or a locator.

question: What is the ILS reference datum point?

options.text: The point where the glide path meets the runway surface
The position of the outer marker on the centre line
The point at which the DH is reached on a Cat I approach
A point about 50 ft above the threshold, on the glide path

explanation: The reference datum is a specified height (about 50 ft) above the intersection of the centre line and the threshold, through which the glide path passes. The figure is published for each airfield.

question: Why may PAPIs and the ILS glide path give slightly different indications close to the runway?

options.text: PAPIs are set for a mean eye height, not the ILS aerial
PAPIs are referenced to the far end of the runway
The ILS glide path is curved near the threshold
PAPIs are set for a steeper angle than the ILS

explanation: Visual approach slope indicators are designed for a mean eye height. The pilot's eye and the aircraft's glide path aerial are at different heights, varying with aircraft size.

question: What does full-scale deflection of the ILS localizer needle represent?

options.text: 0.7° or more off the centre line
5° or more off the centre line
2.5° or more off the centre line
10° or more off the centre line

explanation: In ILS mode the localizer is far more sensitive than a VOR: full scale is 2.5°.

question: On a 5-dot ILS display, what does one dot of localizer deflection represent?
explanation: 2.5° full scale over 5 dots = 0.5° per dot. In VOR mode each dot is 2°.

question: What does full-scale deflection of the glide path needle represent?

options.text: 0.7° or more above or below the glide path
0.35° or more above or below the glide path
2.5° or more above or below the glide path
1.4° or more above or below the glide path

explanation: Glide path full scale is 0.7°, about 0.14° per dot on a 5-dot scale.

question: What is the maximum safe deviation below the glide path?

options.text: Half full scale: 2.5 dots fly down
Half full scale: 2.5 dots fly up
One dot fly up
Full scale: 5 dots fly up

explanation: Half full scale fly up (about 0.35° below the path) is the safe limit. Beyond it, or beyond half-scale on the localizer, go around immediately: terrain clearance may be compromised.

question: A 5-dot ILS display shows the localizer bar 2 dots left of centre. How far is the aircraft from the centre line?

options.text: 1° to the left
0.28° to the right
4° to the right
1° to the right

explanation: Each dot is 0.5°, so 2 dots = 1°. The bar to the left means the centre line is to the left: the aircraft is right of it (fly left).

question: When does an ILS needle centre and show its OFF flag?

options.text: When the aircraft passes the outer marker
When the aircraft is exactly on the centre line or glide path
Outside coverage, transmission fault, or equipment off or failed
When the aircraft is below the decision height

explanation: The OFF flag appears if the aircraft is outside the radiation pattern, there is a transmission fault, or ground or airborne equipment is switched off or has failed. The pilot also confirms the ident.

question: To what height does a Category I ILS facility provide guidance?

options.text: 50 ft (15 m) or less above the threshold
200 ft (60 m) or less above the threshold
To and along the runway surface
100 ft (30 m) or less above the threshold

explanation: Cat I guidance reaches the point where the localizer and glide path intersect at 200 ft or less. Cat II reaches 50 ft or less; Cat III continues to and along the runway.

question: What are the operational minima for a Category I approach?

options.text: DH not below 200 ft, RVR not below 550 m
DH not below 200 ft, RVR not below 800 m
DH not below 100 ft, RVR not below 300 m
DH below 100 ft, RVR not below 200 m

explanation: Cat I: DH ≥ 60 m (200 ft) and RVR ≥ 550 m.

question: What are the operational minima for a Category II approach?

options.text: DH below 100 ft or no DH, RVR not below 200 m
DH below 50 ft or no DH, RVR not below 75 m
DH not below 200 ft, RVR not below 550 m
DH 100 ft to below 200 ft, RVR not below 300 m

explanation: Cat II: DH lower than 200 ft but not lower than 100 ft, RVR at least 300 m.

question: What are the operational minima for a Category IIIA approach?

options.text: DH not below 100 ft, RVR not below 300 m
No DH and no RVR limit
DH below 100 ft or no DH, RVR not below 200 m
DH below 50 ft or no DH, RVR 75 m to 200 m

explanation: Cat IIIA: DH lower than 100 ft (or none) and RVR not less than 200 m.

question: What are the operational minima for a Category IIIB approach?

options.text: DH below 50 ft, RVR not below 300 m
DH below 50 ft or none, RVR 75 m to under 200 m
DH below 100 ft or no DH, RVR not below 200 m
No DH and no RVR limit

explanation: Cat IIIB: DH lower than 50 ft or no DH, RVR from 200 m down to 75 m. Cat IIIC has no DH and no RVR limit.

question: Which approach category has no DH and no RVR limitation?

options.text: Category II
Category IIIB
Category IIIA
Category IIIC

explanation: Cat IIIC has no decision height and no RVR limitation.

question: Which is a condition for approving Category II or III operations?

options.text: The aerodrome is suitably equipped and maintained
The crew have flown the approach in daylight
The aircraft has a glide path receiver only
The approach has a locator at the outer marker

explanation: The aircraft must have suitable flight characteristics, the crew must be qualified and follow laid-down procedures, the aerodrome must be suitably equipped and maintained, and the required safety level must be shown.

question: Which is a limitation of ILS indications?

options.text: Night effect from sky waves beyond about 70 NM from the aerial
Quadrantal error from the airframe
Scalloping: rapid needle swings from reflections
Coastal refraction near the shoreline

explanation: ILS suffers from beam bends (atmospheric), scalloping from reflections (fluctuations too fast to follow) and beam noise from the transmitter or interference. Night effect, quadrantal error and coastal refraction belong to ADF.

question: How can a pilot check the serviceability of the ILS during an approach?

options.text: No warning flags showing, and the ident monitored
The DME counting down steadily
A constant rate of descent of 5 × ground speed
The marker beacon lights coming on in order

explanation: Make sure the flags are not showing and monitor the ident. Loss of the ident means the ILS is unserviceable and the approach must be discontinued immediately.

question: What is the ILS critical area?

options.text: The area beneath the approach path inside the outer marker
An area round the aerials kept clear during all ILS operations
The area within 10 NM where the glide path is protected
An area kept clear only during low-visibility operations

explanation: Vehicles and aircraft inside the critical area would cause unacceptable disturbance to the signal, so they are excluded whenever the ILS is in use.

question: What is the ILS sensitive area?

options.text: The area outside the localizer's ±35° coverage
An area round the aerials kept clear during all ILS operations
An area where false glide slopes may be met
An area beyond the critical area, controlled in low visibility

explanation: The sensitive area extends beyond the critical area. Vehicle and aircraft movement there is controlled during low-visibility operations to prevent interference.

question: Why are Category II/III holding points further from the runway than normal holds?

options.text: To allow faster aircraft to taxi past
To protect the ILS signals from interference
To keep aircraft out of the wake turbulence of landing traffic
To give pilots more time to complete checks

explanation: In Cat II/III operations aircraft are held clear of the sensitive area. These holds are marked "CAT II/III HOLD" and may have a red stop bar.

question: How do snow and heavy rain affect ILS?

options.text: They cause sky waves, which give false glide slopes
They have no effect, because ILS uses VHF and UHF
They attenuate the signals, reducing range and accuracy
They improve range by super-refraction

explanation: Snow and heavy rain attenuate ILS signals, reducing range and degrading accuracy.

question: Why can FM broadcast stations interfere with ILS?

options.text: Their wide bandwidth spills over from just below 108 MHz
They use the same 75 MHz frequency as the markers
They transmit on the glide path's UHF frequencies
Their sky waves reach the localizer at night

explanation: Wide-band FM broadcasts just below 108 MHz can overspill into the navigation band. FM immunity circuits have been mandatory in ILS receivers since the late 1990s.

question: Why may the landing rate be kept relatively low during low-visibility ILS operations?

options.text: Because the markers can be received only by one aircraft
Because the glide path must be re-aligned after each landing
Because ILS can guide only one aircraft at a time
To keep aircraft and vehicles from disturbing the ILS signals

explanation: Aircraft and vehicles near the aerials disturb the signals, so ground movement is restricted and spacing increased, especially in low-visibility procedures.

question: Between which points is the intermediate approach segment flown?

options.text: Up to the initial approach fix
After the final approach fix
Between the IAF and the FAF
From the FAF to the missed approach point

explanation: Initial approach: up to the IAF. Intermediate: from the IAF to the FAF. Final: after the FAF.

question: What are sector safe altitudes (SSAs) on an approach chart?

options.text: Minimum altitudes depending on the sector of arrival
The altitudes at which the glide path is intercepted
The altitudes of the outer and middle markers
The decision heights for each category of approach

explanation: An aircraft should be at or above the SSA for the sector it is approaching from. They are often shown in a circle on the chart.

question: Using the 1-in-60 rule, roughly what height should an aircraft be at 5 NM from touchdown on a 3° glide path?

options.text: 900 ft

explanation: Height ≈ angle × range × 100 = 3 × 5 × 100 = 1 500 ft. The rule slightly underestimates (the exact figure is about 1 590 ft) but is a good gross-error check.

question: Using the 1-in-60 rule, roughly what height should an aircraft be at 4 NM on a 3.5° glide path?
explanation: Height ≈ 3.5 × 4 × 100 = 1 400 ft. Using 3° by mistake gives 1 200 ft.

question: What rate of descent is needed on a 3° glide path at a ground speed of 140 kt?

options.text: 840 ft/min
1 400 ft/min
700 ft/min
420 ft/min

explanation: For 3°, ROD ≈ 5 × ground speed = 5 × 140 = 700 ft/min. Using 3 × GS (420) or 10 × GS (1 400) are the common slips.

question: What rate of descent is needed on a 2.5° glide path at a ground speed of 120 kt?

options.text: 720 ft/min
600 ft/min
300 ft/min
500 ft/min

question: An aircraft on a 3° glide path increases its ground speed. What happens to the required rate of descent?

options.text: It increases in proportion to ground speed
It increases with the square of ground speed
It stays the same, because the angle is fixed
It decreases in proportion to ground speed

explanation: ROD ≈ 5 × GS for a 3° path, so it is directly proportional to ground speed. A tailwind therefore needs a higher rate of descent than a headwind.

question: Why does the 1-in-60 rule slightly underestimate the height and rate of descent on a 3° glide path?

options.text: It ignores the reference datum height of 50 ft
It uses 100 ft per NM per degree instead of about 106
It assumes still air instead of ground speed
It assumes a glide path of 2.5° instead of 3°

explanation: 1 NM = 6 076 ft, and 6 076 / 60 ≈ 101 ft; the true tangent gives about 106 ft per NM per degree. Rounding to 100 makes both results slightly low.

question: An aircraft on a 3° glide path at 150 kt ground speed is 4 NM from touchdown. What height and rate of descent does the 1-in-60 rule give?

options.text: 600 ft and 900 ft/min
1 200 ft and 750 ft/min
1 200 ft and 450 ft/min
1 800 ft and 750 ft/min

explanation: Height ≈ 3 × 4 × 100 = 1 200 ft; ROD ≈ 5 × 150 = 750 ft/min. The exact figures are about 1 270 ft and 800 ft/min.
